## Remarks

The ring maps underlying base change and localization fit into the following commutative squares. Write $f\colon A\to B$ for the given map and $g\colon A\to A'$ for the base-change map.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\Large}, labels={font=\large}]
A \arrow[r,"f"] \arrow[d,"g"'] & B \arrow[d,"i"] & A \arrow[r,"f"] \arrow[d,"\ell_A"'] & B \arrow[d,"\ell_B"] \\
A' \arrow[r,"j"'] & B' & V^{-1}A \arrow[r,"\bar f"'] & U^{-1}B
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here $i(b)=b\otimes1$ and $j(a')=1\otimes a'$. The left square is the tensor-product pushout of [F2]: $i(f(a))=j(g(a))$. On the right, $\ell_A(a)=a/1$, $\ell_B(b)=b/1$, and $\bar f(a/v)=f(a)/f(v)$; the hypothesis $f(V)\subseteq U$ makes $\bar f$ well defined. This square commutes because both paths take $a$ to $f(a)/1$.

For $B'=B\otimes_AA'$, the differential comparison is the commutative triangle of $B'$-modules below. The tensor product in its upper-left corner is over $B$, whereas the two differential modules on the right have different base rings.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, every cell/.append style={font=\Large}, labels={font=\large}]
B'\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A} \arrow[r,"\alpha"] \arrow[dr,"\varphi"',"\cong"] & \Omega_{B'/A} \arrow[d,"q"] \\
& \Omega_{B'/A'}
\end{tikzcd}
```

The map $\alpha$ is the functorial comparison of (3) for $i$, and $q$ sends $\mathrm{d}_{B'/A}x$ to $\mathrm{d}_{B'/A'}x$. Thus $q\alpha=\varphi$: on $1\otimes\mathrm{d}b$, both paths give $\mathrm{d}_{B'/A'}(b\otimes1)$, as in step 2.1. Only $\varphi$ is marked as an isomorphism here. Its inverse is induced by the $A'$-derivation $D(b\otimes a')=a'(1\otimes\mathrm{d}b)$ from step 1.1. For localization, step 1.2 instead uses $D(b/u)=u^{-1}\mathrm{d}b-bu^{-2}\mathrm{d}u$ and identifies $U^{-1}\Omega_{B/A}$ with $\Omega_{U^{-1}B/V^{-1}A}$; [F3] identifies its source with $(U^{-1}B)\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A}$.

These diagrams illustrate the maps already constructed in the proof; the proof is independent of the figures.

## Remarks

For the chase in step 4.1, fix $n$ and abbreviate $J=\mathfrak m^n$, $A=(I\cap J)\otimes_R M$, $B=(I\otimes_R M)\oplus(J\otimes_R M)$ and $C=(I+J)\otimes_R M$. For an ideal $L$, write $\mu_L:L\otimes_R M\to M$ for multiplication. The following diagram displays the right-exact tensor row and its compatibility with multiplication:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large]
A \arrow[r,"\alpha"] \arrow[d,"\mu_{I\cap J}"'] & B \arrow[r,"\beta"] \arrow[d,"\mu_I\oplus\mu_J"] & C \arrow[r] \arrow[d,"\mu_{I+J}"] & 0 \\
M \arrow[r,"\delta"'] & M\oplus M \arrow[r,"\sigma"'] & M \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here $\alpha(x)=(i(x),-j(x))$, where $i:A\to I\otimes_R M$ and $j:A\to J\otimes_R M$ are induced by the ideal inclusions; $\beta$ is induced by addition into $I+J$. The lower maps are $\delta(m)=(m,-m)$ and $\sigma(u,v)=u+v$. Both squares commute: multiplication agrees with each ideal inclusion, and multiplication after addition equals the sum of the two multiplication maps. The top row is exact by [F20]; no injectivity of $\alpha$ is asserted.

For $k\in K$ as in step 4.1, $\mu_{I+J}\beta(k,0)=\mu_I(k)=0$. The injectivity of $\mu_{I+J}$ from step 3.1 gives $\beta(k,0)=0$, so exactness lifts $(k,0)$ to some $x\in A$. Thus $i(x)=k$ and $j(x)=0$, and $\mu_{I\cap J}(x)=\mu_Jj(x)=0$. The diagram illustrates this lift and its sign convention; the rigorous proof above is independent of the figure.

Put $W=U\cap V$ and suppress the common coefficient ring $R$. With the orientations on $U$, $V$ and $W$ restricted from $M$, the commuting ladder is

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large, /tikz/font=\Large, labels={font=\large}]
H_c^p(W) \arrow[r, "{(e_U,-e_V)}"] \arrow[d, "D_W"'] & H_c^p(U)\oplus H_c^p(V) \arrow[r, "e_U+e_V"] \arrow[d, "D_U\oplus D_V"] & H_c^p(M) \arrow[r, "\delta"] \arrow[d, "D_M"] & H_c^{p+1}(W) \arrow[d, "D_W"] \\
H_{n-p}(W) \arrow[r, "{(i_{U*},-i_{V*})}"'] & H_{n-p}(U)\oplus H_{n-p}(V) \arrow[r, "i_{U*}+i_{V*}"'] & H_{n-p}(M) \arrow[r, "{(-1)^{p+1}\partial}"'] & H_{n-p-1}(W)
\end{tikzcd}
```

Here the first horizontal maps use the inclusions of $W$ into $U$ and $V$, and the second use the inclusions of $U$ and $V$ into $M$. Both rows are segments of exact sequences. The rightmost vertical map uses cohomological degree $p+1$, so its target is $H_{n-p-1}(W)$. The first two squares express open naturality from step 1.1. For the last square, the connector convention is $[z_U+z_V]\mapsto[\partial z_U]$; steps 6.1–7.1 give $\partial D_M=(-1)^{p+1}D_W\delta$, hence $(-1)^{p+1}\partial D_M=D_W\delta$. ## Remarks

The fiber-product square defining the exchange mate is Cartesian:

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, scale=1.5, transform shape]
T=A\times_M B \arrow[r,"a"] \arrow[d,"b"'] & A \arrow[d,"q"] \\
B \arrow[r,"u"'] & M
\end{tikzcd}
```

The graph factorization in step 3.1 fits into the following two Cartesian squares. Here $\Gamma_q(x)=(x,q(x))$, $\theta(x,y)=(x,y)$, and $\Delta(m)=(m,m)$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large, row sep=large, scale=1.5, transform shape]
T \arrow[r,"a"] \arrow[d,hook,"\theta"'] & A \arrow[r,"q"] \arrow[d,hook,"\Gamma_q"] & M \arrow[d,hook,"\Delta"] \\
A\times B \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}_A\times u"'] & A\times M \arrow[r,"{(q,\mathrm{id}_M)}"'] & M\times M
\end{tikzcd}
```

The bottom composite is $F=(q,u)$, while the top composite is $qa=ub$. Thus the outer rectangle identifies $T$ with $F^{-1}(\Delta(M))$, as used in step 2.1. Pulling the supported morphism $g_\Delta$ first through the right square and then through the left gives $g_F$ by the proper-base-change identifications in steps 2.1 and 3.1. The factorization of $q$ itself is $q=\operatorname{pr}_2\circ\Gamma_q$. These diagrams record the supports and maps only; the orientation, adjunction and counit arguments remain those of the proof, independently of the illustrations.

Consider a cartesian square with $f:X\to Y$ proper and $g:Y'\to Y$ flat of pure relative dimension $n$, and write $f':X'=X\times_Y Y'\to Y'$ and $g':X'\to X$. For an integral $d$-dimensional $V\subseteq X$, put $W=\overline{f(V)}$ and $e=\dim V-\dim W$. If $e>0$, both $g^*f_*[V]$ and $f'_*g'^*[V]$ are zero: every component of the flat pullback of $V$ has dimension $d+n$, while its image has dimension at most $\dim W+n<d+n$. If $e=0$, set $m=[k(V):k(W)]$. For each component $W_i$ of $g^{-1}(W)$, let $C_i$ be the Artinian local ring of $W\times_Y Y'$ at its generic point. Flat pullback gives coefficient $\ell(C_i)$ on $[W_i]$. The generic algebra of $V\times_Y Y'$ over $C_i$ is $C_i\otimes_{k(W)}k(V)$, a free $C_i$-module of rank $m$. Decomposing it into its Artinian local factors shows that the sum of the generic lengths of the components above $W_i$, weighted by their function-field degrees over $k(W_i)$, is $m\ell(C_i)$. These are precisely the coefficients of $[W_i]$ in $f'_*g'^*[V]$ and $g^*f_*[V]$, respectively. Hence the base-change identity holds on cycles and therefore on Chow groups. Finally, if $f$ is finite flat of constant degree $n$ between integral schemes of the same dimension, then $f$ is dominant and $[k(X):k(Y)]=n$, so $f_*[X]=n[Y]$ by step 1.1. ## Remarks

The base-change assertion in step 4.1 involves two squares. The first is
Cartesian, with $X'=X\times_Y Y'$ and the two projections $g'$ and $f'$:

```tikzcd
[column sep=large, row sep=large, font=\Large]
X'=X\times_Y Y' \arrow[r, "\textstyle g'"] \arrow[d, "\textstyle f'"']
& X \arrow[d, "\textstyle f"] \\
Y' \arrow[r, "\textstyle g"'] & Y
```

Here $f\circ g'=g\circ f'$. The vertical maps are proper, and the horizontal
maps are flat of pure relative dimension $n$. Pushforward follows the vertical
arrows, whereas flat pullback reverses the horizontal arrows. Thus the second
square has the following directions and dimension indices:

```tikzcd
[column sep=huge, row sep=large, font=\Large]
Z_d(X) \arrow[r, "\textstyle g'^*"] \arrow[d, "\textstyle f_*"']
& Z_{d+n}(X') \arrow[d, "\textstyle f'_*"] \\
Z_d(Y) \arrow[r, "\textstyle g^*"'] & Z_{d+n}(Y')
```

Its commutativity is $f'_*g'^*=g^*f_*$, proved in step 4.1; the same square
holds with $A$ in place of $Z$. The degree is dimension, so proper pushforward
preserves the index and flat pullback increases it by $n$. This does not
assert that proper pushforward preserves codimension. For an integral
$V\subseteq X$, the equal-dimensional case retains the full coefficient
$m=[k(V):k(W)]$, where $W=\overline{f(V)}$: the generic-length computation in
step 4.1 gives $m\ell(C_i)$ at each component $W_i$ above $W$. No assumption
that these field degrees or generic lengths equal one is made, including
over a nonclosed field. In the dimension-drop case both routes give zero.
The diagrams illustrate the maps and their grading; the proof above remains
independent of them.

steps.before: 8.1 Sections of smooth morphisms. Let $s:T\to P$ be a section of a smooth morphism $P\to T$ of constant relative dimension $r$, with $T$ locally Noetherian. Near a point $t\in T$, [F8] factors $P\to T$ Zariski locally as an étale morphism $P'\to\mathbb A^r_T=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_T[x_1,\dots,x_r]$ followed by the projection, after shrinking around $s(t)$ and $t$; by [F7] the étale morphism is flat. The composite $T\to P'\to\mathbb A^r_T$ is the graph of the $T$-point with coordinates $c_i=s^*(x_i)$. This graph is cut out by the regular sequence $x_1-c_1,\dots,x_r-c_r$: after quotienting by the first $i$ terms, the next element is a monic linear polynomial in a new variable and hence a nonzerodivisor over any base ring. Pulling the graph back along the flat étale map $P'\to\mathbb A^r_T$ gives a regular immersion $Q=T\times_{\mathbb A^r_T}P'\hookrightarrow P'$ of codimension $r$, and $Q\to T$ is étale. The section factors through a section $T\to Q$ of this étale morphism. By [F8], after shrinking near the chosen point, this section is described by a standard étale chart $\operatorname{Spec}((A[z]/(P))_g)\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $z\mapsto a$, $P(a)=0$ and $P'(a)$ a unit. Factoring $P(z)=(z-a)Q_0(z)$ gives $Q_0(a)=P'(a)$; after restricting to the open neighborhood where $Q_0$ is invertible, the equation $P(z)=0$ forces $z=a$, so the section is an open immersion there. Hence near its image in $P'$, the pulled-back regular equations cut out $s(T)$, proving that $s$ is a regular immersion of codimension $r$. These equations remain regular after every base change $T'\to T$, since the section of the smooth base change $P\times_TT'\to T'$ is again locally obtained by this graph construction, including when $T'$ is singular. The normal bundle also commutes with base change: for a section of a smooth morphism, the conormal bundle identifies with $s^*\Omega^1_{P/T}$, and this relative differential bundle pulls back to $s'^*\Omega^1_{(P\times_TT')/T'}$. Hence the codimension and normal bundle are preserved by arbitrary base change on $T$. [F7, F8, algebra] ∎

This graph is cut out by the regular sequence $x_1-c_1,\dots,x_r-c_r$: after quotienting by the first $i$ terms, the next element is a monic linear polynomial in a new variable and hence a nonzerodivisor over any base ring. Pulling the graph back along the flat étale map $P'\to\mathbb A^r_T$ gives a regular immersion $Q=T\times_{\mathbb A^r_T}P'\hookrightarrow P'$ of codimension $r$, and $Q\to T$ is étale. The section factors through a section $T\to Q$ of this étale morphism. By [F8], after shrinking near the chosen point, this section is described by a standard étale chart $\operatorname{Spec}((A[z]/(P))_g)\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $z\mapsto a$, $P(a)=0$ and $P'(a)$ a unit. Factoring $P(z)=(z-a)Q_0(z)$ gives $Q_0(a)=P'(a)$; after restricting to the open neighborhood where $Q_0$ is invertible, the equation $P(z)=0$ forces $z=a$, so the section is an open immersion there. Hence near its image in $P'$, the pulled-back regular equations cut out $s(T)$, proving that $s$ is a regular immersion of codimension $r$. These equations remain regular after every base change $T'\to T$, since the section of the smooth base change $P\times_TT'\to T'$ is again locally obtained by this graph construction, including when $T'$ is singular. The normal bundle also commutes with base change: for a section of a smooth morphism, the conormal bundle identifies with $s^*\Omega^1_{P/T}$, and this relative differential bundle pulls back to $s'^*\Omega^1_{(P\times_TT')/T'}$. Hence the codimension and normal bundle are preserved by arbitrary base change on $T$. [F7, F8, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

For a fixed coefficient group $G$, the following exact-row fragment displays
all three types of naturality square, including the degree-lowering connector.
Here $i_*$ is induced by subspace inclusion, $q_*$ by the quotient of chain
complexes, $f_A=f|_A:A\to B$, and $f_{\mathrm{rel},*}$ is the relative homology
map induced by $[c]\mapsto[f_\#c]$.

```tikzcd
\begin{tikzcd}[font=\Large, labels={font=\large}, column sep=large, row sep=large]
H_n(A;G) \arrow[r, "i_*"] \arrow[d, "(f_A)_*"'] &
H_n(X;G) \arrow[r, "q_*"] \arrow[d, "f_*"] &
H_n(X,A;G) \arrow[r, "\delta_{X,A}"] \arrow[d, "f_{\mathrm{rel},*}"] &
H_{n-1}(A;G) \arrow[d, "(f_A)_*"] \\
H_n(B;G) \arrow[r, "i_*"'] &
H_n(Y;G) \arrow[r, "q_*"'] &
H_n(Y,B;G) \arrow[r, "\delta_{Y,B}"'] &
H_{n-1}(B;G)
\end{tikzcd}
```

The right square says $(f_A)_*\delta_{X,A}=\delta_{Y,B}f_{\mathrm{rel},*}$.
For a relative cycle represented by $c$, the connector is represented by
$\partial c$ in the subspace, and $f_\#\partial c=\partial f_\#c$ gives this
identity with no extra sign. These are relative chain quotients, not a claim
identifying relative homology with the homology of a quotient space. The proof
above is independent of the diagram.

Write $P=\mathbb P(\mathcal E)$ and denote the isomorphism in the statement
by $\Phi_d$. Proper pushforward detects its last summand, as the following
commutative square illustrates:

```tikzcd

  \arrow[r, "\textstyle\Phi_d", "\textstyle\sim"']
  \arrow[d, "\textstyle\mathrm{pr}_{r-1}"']
```

$A_{d+i+r-1}(P)$, and capping with $\xi^i$ then lands in the common group

pushforward operations in step 2.1 apply after the already detected
coefficients have vanished in the relation; the square asserts no simultaneous
extraction of all coefficients. For $r=1$, it reduces to
$\pi_*\pi^*=\operatorname{id}$ with $\xi^0$ the identity operation.

proof above remains independent of it.
